name: Genesis
v: Abraham was old now, deep into his years, and the LORD had blessed him in every way.
He said to his chief servant, the one who ran the whole estate, "Put your hand under my thigh.
I want you to swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and earth, that you will not find a wife for my son from among these Canaanite women I live beside.
You will go back — back to my homeland, to my own people — and find a wife for my son Isaac there."
The servant said, "But what if the woman won't come with me? What if she refuses to leave her country? Should I take your son back to the land you came from?"
"No," Abraham said. "Never take my son back there.

The LORD, the God of heaven, who pulled me out of my father's house and away from the land of my birth, who spoke to me and swore an oath — 'To your offspring I will give this land' — He will send His messenger ahead of you. You will find a wife for my son there.
And if the woman refuses to follow you, you're released from the oath. Just don't take my son back to that place."
So the servant placed his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to do exactly what he'd said.
He took ten of his master's camels and loaded them with the best of everything Abraham owned, and he set out — heading north to Aram-naharaim, to the city of Nahor.
When he arrived, he made the camels kneel outside the city by the well. It was evening — the hour when the women came out to draw water.
Then he prayed: "LORD, God of my master Abraham — let it happen today. Show kindness to my master Abraham.
Look — I'm standing here at the spring, and the daughters of the townspeople are coming out to draw water.

Let this be the sign: when I ask a young woman, 'Please tip your jar so I can drink,' and she says, 'Drink — and I'll water your camels too' — let her be the one You've chosen for Your servant Isaac. That's how I'll know You've shown kindness to my master."
He hadn't even finished praying when Rebekah came out, her jar on her shoulder. She was the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, who was the wife of Abraham's brother Nahor.
The girl was stunning — a virgin, untouched. She went down to the spring, filled her jar, and came back up.
The servant ran to meet her. "Please — let me drink a little water from your jar."
"Drink, sir," she said, and quickly lowered the jar into her hands and gave him a drink.
When she'd finished giving him water, she said, "I'll draw for your camels too — until they've had their fill."
She emptied her jar into the trough, ran back to the well, drew again — and again, and again, until every camel had drunk.
The man watched her in silence, studying her, wondering whether the LORD had made his journey succeed.
When the camels finished drinking, he took out a gold nose-ring — half a shekel — and two gold bracelets weighing ten shekels,
and said, "Whose daughter are you? Tell me — is there room at your father's house for us to spend the night?"
"I'm the daughter of Bethuel," she said, "the son Milcah bore to Nahor.
And yes — we have plenty of straw and feed, and room to stay the night."
The man dropped to his knees and worshiped the LORD.
"Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not abandoned His loyal love and faithfulness to my master. The LORD led me right to the house of my master's kin."
The girl ran home and told her mother's household everything.
Rebekah had a brother named Laban. Laban ran out to the man at the spring.

He had seen the nose-ring and the bracelets on his sister's arms, and heard her say, "This is what the man told me." So he came out — and there was the man, still standing with the camels by the spring.
"Come in," Laban said, "blessed of the LORD. Why are you standing out here? I've prepared the house — and a place for the camels."
So the man went in. They unloaded the camels, gave them straw and feed, and brought water for him and his men to wash their feet.

Food was set before him, but he said, "I can't eat until I've said what I came to say."

"Speak," Laban said.
"I am Abraham's servant," he began.
"The LORD has blessed my master abundantly — he has become a great man. He's given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys.
And Sarah, my master's wife, bore him a son in her old age — and to that son he has given everything he owns.
"My master made me swear an oath: 'Do not get a wife for my son from the Canaanite women whose land I live in.
Go to my father's house, to my clan, and find a wife for my son there.'
"I said to my master, 'What if the woman won't come back with me?'
"He said, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send His messenger with you and make your journey succeed. You will find a wife for my son from my clan, from my father's house.
Only then will you be released from my oath — when you've gone to my clan. And if they refuse to give her to you, you're free from the oath.'
"So today I came to the spring and prayed: 'LORD, God of my master Abraham — if You would now make the journey I've come on succeed —
here I am, standing at the spring. Let it be that the young woman who comes out to draw water, the one I ask, "Please give me a little water from your jar,"
and she answers, "Drink — and I'll draw for your camels too" — let her be the wife the LORD has chosen for my master's son.'
"Before I'd even finished praying in my heart, Rebekah came out, her jar on her shoulder. She went down to the spring and drew water, and I said to her, 'Please — let me drink.'
She lowered her jar at once and said, 'Drink — and I'll water your camels too.' So I drank, and she watered the camels.
"I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' She said, 'The daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor and Milcah.' So I put the ring in her nose and the bracelets on her arms,
and I bowed down and worshiped the LORD. I blessed the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who had led me straight to the daughter of my master's kin for his son.
"So now — if you intend to show loyalty and faithfulness to my master, tell me. And if not, tell me that too, so I can turn one way or the other."
Laban and Bethuel answered, "This is from the LORD. We can't say anything to you, good or bad.
Here is Rebekah. Take her and go. Let her be the wife of your master's son, just as the LORD has spoken."
When Abraham's servant heard this, he fell to the ground before the LORD.
Then he brought out silver and gold jewelry and clothing and gave them to Rebekah, and gave precious gifts to her brother and her mother.
He and the men with him ate and drank and stayed the night. In the morning he said, "Send me back to my master."
But her brother and her mother said, "Let the girl stay with us a few more days — say, ten. Then she can go."
He said, "Don't hold me back. The LORD has made my journey succeed. Send me on so I can return to my master."
They said, "Let's call the girl and ask her."

So they called Rebekah and said, "Will you go with this man?"

"I will," she said.
So they sent off Rebekah their sister with her nurse, along with Abraham's servant and his men.

And they blessed Rebekah:

"Our sister — may you become
the mother of thousands upon thousands.
May your offspring seize the gates
of those who hate them."
Then Rebekah and her young women got up, mounted the camels, and followed the man. The servant took Rebekah and went.
Isaac had come back from the region of Beer-lahai-roi — he was living in the Negev.
One evening he went out into the field to meditate, and he looked up — and there were camels coming.
Rebekah looked up too, and when she saw Isaac, she slipped down from her camel.

"Who is that man walking out in the field to meet us?" she asked the servant.

"That is my master," he said.

So she took her veil and covered herself.
The servant told Isaac everything he'd done.
And Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother Sarah. He took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted, at last, after his mother's death.

com.d:
# Genesis 24: The Providence of Patient Love

This remarkable chapter reveals how God works through the ordinary faithfulness of his people to accomplish his purposes, teaching us that providence operates not through dramatic miracles alone but through attentive listening, humble service, and trust in divine ordering.

Abraham's servant undertakes an arduous journey to find a wife for Isaac, knowing only that God will guide him. What strikes us immediately is his method: he doesn't rush ahead with his own schemes but pauses at a well and prays for a specific sign. This is not presumption dressed as faith, but genuine dependence—he asks God to confirm his path through circumstances. When Rebekah appears and acts with the exact kindness he requested, he worships, recognizing God's hand in what might otherwise seem coincidental.

This story speaks to how divine guidance often comes not through booming voices but through the alignment of our faithful actions with God's gentle orchestration. The servant remains utterly devoted to his master's mission, traveling miles away from home without knowing the outcome. His reliability and trustworthiness become the very instruments through which God works. When he finally presents his testimony to Rebekah's family, his careful attention to detail—what God did, how he prayed, what happened—demonstrates that faith notices and narrates God's faithfulness.

The chapter also shows us something tender about God's care for the marginal. Rebekah, a young woman far from home, receives water and kindness. She discovers herself chosen, elevated, part of a covenant family. God sees her. His providence includes her thriving.

For those of us navigating uncertainty, this passage invites us to the same posture: pray specifically, remain faithful in the small things assigned to us, watch for God's confirmation, and trust that he cares about the details of our stories. Providence means we need not anxiously orchestrate our lives; we can serve faithfully where we are while remaining alert to how God guides.

What area of your life invites you to pray specifically and then watch attentively for God's guidance?
com.s:
Genesis 24 stands as the longest chapter in the book of Genesis and represents one of the most artfully constructed narratives in the Hebrew Bible. This account of securing a bride for Isaac unfolds during the final phase of Abraham's life, functioning as a pivotal transition text that ensures the continuation of the covenant promises through the proper lineage. The narrative likely reflects patriarchal marriage customs of the early second millennium BCE, where endogamy—marriage within one's kinship group—served to preserve family identity, inheritance rights, and religious distinctiveness.

The chapter opens with Abraham commissioning his senior servant, traditionally identified as Eliezer of Damascus though unnamed here, to undertake the momentous task of finding a wife for Isaac. The oath-taking ceremony involves placing the hand under Abraham's "thigh" (*yarek*), a euphemism likely referring to the reproductive organs, signifying that the servant swears by Abraham's descendants—the very posterity at stake in this mission. Abraham's insistence that the bride not be taken from the Canaanites reflects theological concerns about maintaining covenant purity rather than mere ethnic prejudice, anticipating later Deuteronomic prohibitions against intermarriage.

The servant's prayer at the well introduces the key term *hesed*, often translated "steadfast love" or "loving-kindness," which appears three times in this chapter. When Rebekah appears and fulfills the precise conditions the servant had proposed, he recognizes divine *hesed* at work, acknowledging that YHWH has guided (*nahah*) his journey. This verb of guidance emphasizes providential direction throughout the narrative.

Structurally, the chapter employs extensive repetition—the servant recounts the entire episode to Rebekah's family—a literary device that emphasizes the significance of these events and demonstrates divine orchestration. Some scholars have noted this repetition as evidence of source compilation, while others view it as deliberate narrative artistry common in ancient Near Eastern literature.

Rebekah emerges as a remarkably active figure, demonstrating initiative, hospitality, and ultimately consenting to the marriage with the decisive declaration "I will go" (*elek*). Her characterization balances agency with providential determination, establishing her as a worthy matriarch. The chapter concludes with Isaac's love for Rebekah providing comfort after Sarah's death, thus completing one generational transition while inaugurating the next.
com.p:
Genesis 24 unfolds approximately 2,000 years before Christ, roughly 1900 BC, in the aftermath of Sarah's death recorded in the previous chapter. Abraham is now advanced in years, and Isaac has reached marriageable age. This pivotal narrative stands within the patriarchal period, between the Abrahamic covenant's establishment and the eventual descent into Egypt, firmly planted in that critical epoch where God was forming a covenant family through whom all nations would be blessed.

Within the grand redemptive arc, this chapter advances the promise from Abraham to the next generation. The seed through whom blessing flows must continue, and that continuation requires a bride. Here the Spirit of God pulls back the veil on a profound mystery that would not be fully understood until the advent of Christ and His church.

Abraham, the aged father, sends his most trusted servant—unnamed but faithful—to obtain a bride for his beloved son. The servant journeys to a far country, bearing gifts and the authority of his master's name. He does not speak of himself but testifies of the son's glory, declaring that the father has given all things into the son's hand. Rebekah is found at the well, responds to the servant's word, receives his gifts, and willingly leaves her father's house to journey toward a bridegroom she has never seen. Isaac, meanwhile, has come from Beer Lahai Roi—"the well of the Living One who sees me"—and goes out into the field at evening to meet her.

The typological pattern blazes with light. The Father sends the Spirit into the world to call out a Bride for His beloved Son. The Spirit does not speak of Himself but glorifies Christ, testifying of all the Father has given Him. The Bride is found at the well of living water, hears the testimony, receives the earnest gifts, and forsakes all to follow One she has not yet seen but loves. The Son, who has passed through death and emerged from the place of resurrection life, goes forth to meet His Bride.

This ancient narrative prophetically frames the entire church age. We are Rebekah, called from among the nations, betrothed but not yet united, traveling toward the evening hour when we shall see Him face to face. The Spirit adorns us with gifts, assuring us of our Bridegroom's wealth and love. We journey by faith, not by sight, until that glorious moment when the heavens part and we behold the One for whom we have waited. The marriage supper of the Lamb approaches.
